2.text: istic story, which happened in the Chaun country in the year 1894, and was

3.text: told to me by a man who knew the participants. I give it in his own words: —

4.text: “A reindeer-breeder lived in a lone camp in the middle of the tundra. He had an assistant

5.text: in the camp. This man, Amonaiˊhɪn by name, had a wife with a very active tongue. He was a

6.text: great eˊrmečɪn, but a poor herdsman, too lazy to run around the herd. Therefore the master

7.text: almost stopped slaughtering reindeer for him. In reality, the master said to himself, ‘This one is

8.text: quite worthless.’ Moreover, Amonaiˊhɪn did not like to listen to remonstrances, and the master

9.text: felt uncomfortable about telling him anything. Then Amonaiˊhɪn’s wife began to reproach him.

10.text: ‘We suffer from hunger, living with such a wealthy reindeer-breeder. We are just on the verge of

11.text: dying a shameful death. I say, I should have him killed.’ At first the husband would not listen.

12.text: At last, however, he paid attention to these words. Then he followed the master to the reindeer-

13.text: herd. They remained together with the herd. There was a hill there. The assistant said, ‘Let

14.text: us climb the hill and look around for better pasture.’ — ‘All right,’ said the master. They climbed

15.text: the hill. The master walked in front, and the assistant a little behind. Amonaiˊhɪn caught the

16.text: master from behind. He had a knife ready in his sleeve. With this knife he cut open his master’s

17.text: abdomen. Then he loosened his grip; and the wounded master tried to run, but fell to the ground.

18.text: Amonaiˊhɪn left him there, still alive, and went home. The night passed. Not until morning did

19.text: he say to his wife, ‘Well, I have finished with my quarry. Now it is your turn to do something

20.text: with yours.’ The wife said, ‘Ugh, do it all!’ — ‘Nay, but your plain words were, “Let every one

21.text: of us have a quarry of his own.”’ The woman sighed. ‘Then let it be so!’ She sharpened her

22.text: knife, and hid it in her sleeve. Then she went to the front house. The woman of the front

23.text: house, who was a girl, was making fire. She stabbed her from behind, but could not kill her,

24.text: the girl being a shaman. Therefore the murderess cut all the ligaments on her arms and legs.

25.text: The girl became bereft of all power of motion. Her little brother, who still wore a combination-

26.text: suit, tried to flee. The murderess ran after him and stabbed him. Then she broke the front

27.text: house, cut to pieces all the poles and sledges, and made of this wood a large pile, adding some

28.text: branches of bushes. After that she put the two bodies on the pile, and they were burned.

30.text: “The air was quite motionless, as is often the case in spring. The smoke rose upward in

31.text: a long column, and was seen from afar. The Maritime traders travelling with dogs happened to

32.text: pass by just at this time, and saw the smoke. So they turned in to see, and beheld the pile.

33.text: Amonaiˊhɪn felt uneasy. He could not even deny anything. ‘Well, well, such a thing has hap-

34.text: pened here. Maybe I shall also slay both of you. Truly, you would not be able to hold your

35.text: peace, would you?’ — ‘Oh, yes! we should.’ They began to make bows to him quite low, as to

36.text: a great officer. ‘We shall keep quiet. Only give us some provisions.’ They spent a night there.

37.text: All the time they talked in this way. The next morning he slaughtered reindeer and gave them

38.text: as much as their dogs could carry. When they came home, they caused a great sensation with

39.text: their tale. The next year the kinsmen of the slain man found the murderer and slew him. His

40.text: wife and his son were left untouched. The woman’s name is Tñe-čeiˊvuñe.”¹

41.text: In another case of a similar kind, the assistant, with the aid of his cousin,

42.text: killed the master of the camp. Then he staid with the family of the slain

43.text: man and slaughtered reindeer for his own use. For a long time the murderer

44.text: slaughtered their reindeer, until the family became quite poor, and finally lost

45.text: their entire herd. Then he left them and went elsewhere.²

46.text: The folk-stories also contain similar cases. Most characteristic is one

47.text: described in the tale of “Eleˊndi and His Sons:” —
